article.title: Decline of American Empire
article.author: Tom Engelhardt
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Only recently, after a mere two decades of intermittent conflict (with three years off ), the last U.S. troops finally withdrew from... yes, can you believe it?... Iraq! Don’t be shocked, since we’re talking about a country significantly less than 7,000 miles from our shores. Honestly, that’s next to nothing if you remember that, in my youth, the U.S. was fighting a 20-year-long war in Vietnam (and Laos and Cambodia) about 9,000 miles from Washington, D.C. The conflict in Iraq didn’t even last that long. After all, the U.S. didn’t launch its war there until its invasion of 2003, which, in the great scope of time, was essentially yesterday. And I certainly can’t complain about any of that. After all, this country’s distant wars have always given me something to do. Once upon a time—on April 3, 1968, in fact— I even turned in my draft card at an antiwar demonstration on Boston Common to protest that very war in Vietnam. (In those days, of course, the U.S. Army wasn’t an all-volunteer outfit.) And some weeks later, I wrote a letter refusing a National Defense Foreign Language Fellowship to fund my study of Chinese history at Harvard graduate school. I still have a xerox of that letter, which reads in part: “On the afternoon of April 3rd, on returning to my apartment, I found a letter from Harvard University offering me a National Defense Foreign Language Fellowship to study Chinese language and history at Harvard in the ‘national interest’ for a government which has for years been flagrantly working against that interest. The mistake in a sense had been mine. I had applied for the grant, thoughtlessly, and for that I apologize. Nonetheless, arriving as it did, at the moment it did in my life, it seemed like a bribe, (even if obviously an unconscious one). ‘You made your silly gesture,’ it said, ‘now forget it and take this money.’ ‘There are no strings attached,’ said my friends and perhaps not... “It is, I have been told, innocuous, fairly administered, and helpful to the promotion of learning. I won’t bother to dispute this. But like so many first steps, so many deals we enter where we are assured there are ‘no strings,’ we are later surprised to find ourselves trapped. I look at this first step and it seems so harmless, in fact so inviting; but I look at the results in the field of modern Chinese studies and I say ‘no,’ I will take my chances another way with few regrets.” Related: Trump Is Fighting the Future—and China Is Winning As it happened, within months of writing that letter I had left my studies at Harvard and become a printer—yes, a printer!—at what in that mobilized antiwar moment was known as a “movement printshop.” A mere 58 years later, in an America without a draft, I have nothing (other than this Substack, of course) to turn in—or even turn to— in order to protest my government’s latest war against Iran. Still, don’t you find it strange that, more than half a century ago, my country’s military was fighting in Vietnam (and Laos and Cambodia), while almost six decades later, things have indeed grown so much more logical, as Tehran, the capital of Iran, is a mere 6,300 or so miles from Washington, D.C. Give us another half century, and (if planet Earth is even a livable place anymore), my country (if it still exists) could be fighting a war a mere 3,000 or so miles from its shores and then... but I won’t go on, since I’m sure you can do the math at least as well as I can. (It was never my strong point!) Buy the Book Oh, and in the coming months, in the age of Donald Trump and the “ Donroe Doctrine “ when anything is possible, we could break all the rules of American warfare (with the exception of the invasion of the tiny Caribbean island of Grenada in 1983 and “our” president’s brief militarized leap into Venezuela to seize its leader and his wife as this year began) and invade Cuba , a mere 90 to 100 (instead of 6,000 to 9,000) miles off the coast of Florida. After all, simply destroying endless numbers of boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean is anything but enough! And if you don’t find that distinctly upbeat as a near-future possibility, then what in the world would be? Heading Down, Down, Down On the other side of the coin (yes, I just flipped it!), in 1968, when I wrote that letter, former Vice President Lyndon Johnson, who became president after John F. Kennedy was assassinated, was still “my” president. Today, a mere 58 years later, it’s (gulp!) Donald J. Trump who, unbelievably enough, won his second term in office in 2024 with 49.8% of the national vote—and just in case you’ve forgotten, that was 3.4% more than he got when he won the 2016 election (while losing the popular vote count to Hillary Clinton!), and almost 3% more than his count in 2020 when he lost to Joe Biden (the only candidate in any of the last three elections to get more than half the vote— 51.3% ). And if all of that doesn’t tell you what you need to know about the downhill slope of American politics and history (or perhaps even of politics and history globally), then let me know what might. In short, the single most powerful country on the planet is now ruled by a distinct madman who never won 50% of the vote, which also tells you all too much about this increasingly divided country and endangered world of ours. And if that’s the path we’re on (as it seems to be) on this distinctly overheating planet of ours in which wars still rage from Ukraine to Gaza to Somalia, pouring fossil fuels into the atmosphere (as will the future spread of AI data centers ), try for a moment to imagine the nature (and acts) of a president (if that even still proves to be his— and yes, it will probably still be a HIM as in His Imperial Majesty—title) in whatever passes for the United States of America 20 or 30 years from now, when we may be fighting our wars so much closer to home (or even right in this country). Phew, that sentence exhausted me! Imagine going back in history and telling George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, or Franklin Delano Roosevelt (all of whom were wartime presidents) about this Trumpian wartime moment and planet of ours. Or maybe just return to 1956, when my parents—my father having been in the Air Force in World War II—voted for Democratic candidate Adlai Stevenson and yet Dwight D. Eisenhower, the former Supreme Allied Commander in Europe in World War II, won his second term in office and that seemed like bad news to us then. Of course, our present world—if someone had even been able to describe it to us then—would have been inconceivable, if not the most ridiculous science fiction plot ever. (If somehow Eisenhower or Johnson were to return and win a presidential election now, it would be a hallelujah moment, which tells you just how far we’ve come in the last nearly three-quarters of a century.) Related: Donald Trump and a World at the Boiling Point Once upon a time, nothing could have convinced me that Donald Trump—had you described him to me then (assuming he’s even describable in the normal sense of the term)—could possibly have been elected president or that this country would functionally go to war ( economically at least ) with our neighbor Canada. Had you made up such a plot, you would then have been categorized as a raging idiot. I would have simply laughed you out of the room. That’s our future? Give me a break! Whatever my country’s problems and disturbing acts were once upon a time, the present moment would then have been the single lousiest joke imaginable. And yet here we are in that once inconceivable future on a planet slowly going down the tubes—and it’s hard even to imagine how to protest it all, especially “our” president. Is there anything left that could be turned in to protest this hell on earth we all too literally find ourselves in? And don’t forget to add one more all-American thing: imagine that you had told me on that April 3rd so long ago that, 58 years later, our country, led by a maniac named Donald Trump, would be fighting yet another war thousands of miles away. Or what if you had said that this world of ours more generally would still be engulfed in war from Ukraine to the Middle East to—thank you again, Washington!— Somalia ? And what if you had asked me what we should make of a planetary power that, for endless decades, has fought wars in distant lands, but whose president now seems all too intent on bringing war ever closer to home? Given the history of the United States in the last century or so, that—and he—couldn’t be more striking symbols of decline on a planet that itself is going down in a big-time fashion. The madness of Donald Trump as president of the United States (twice!), though seldom thought of that way, should undoubtedly be seen as a sign of the once greatest imperial power going down, down, down in a big-time way and potentially taking so much else down with it. I wonder what letter I would write today, if I were in my early twenties and facing just such a world? Tom's Substack
